reader.title: Killing of a man suspected of being "Railroad Bill" near Chipley, Georgia
bases: A man sought as a suspected outlaw was shot dead near Chipley by Willis Garner, described as a member of the sheriff's posse (A1, A6), or by a young man accompanying a deputy constable (A2), while they tried to take him.

The man was killed (A1, A2), but the reports describe an attempted arrest by a posse member or a deputy constable's companion who fired after being shot (A1, A2), not a group killing outside the law; the party's size is given as two (A2) or left vague as a posse or 'four-cornered fight' (A1, A7).

Two separate Montgomery dispatches of Aug. 16 (A1, A2), with different wording and details, agree that a Black man was shot dead near Chipley after wounding the man who killed him; the dead man's identity is contested (A2, A5).

summary.text: The killing of a man suspected of being "Railroad Bill" near Chipley, Georgia, took place on August 15, 1895, when Willis Garner, described as a member of a sheriff's posse, shot a Black man in a deserted house.
The man had been taken for the Alabama outlaw known as "Railroad Bill," but railroad men who viewed his body in Montgomery said it was not the outlaw.
A letter from Chipley later identified him as a Mobile laborer named Thomas, against whom no crime was charged in Mobile.

"Railroad Bill," named in a Montgomery dispatch as Morris Slater, was described in the white press as "the notorious desperado, murderer and train robber of South Alabama," with a reward of $1,250 on his head.

According to the Birmingham Age-Herald, a deputy constable at Chipley and a young acquaintance heard that a Black man answering the outlaw's description had been staying for a day or two in an abandoned hut nearby.
On Thursday afternoon the two men went to the hut and called on the man to surrender.
By their account he answered with a pistol shot that struck the young man, named in other reports as Willis Garner, in the abdomen.
Garner fell, then fired back, and a Winchester bullet passed through the man's chest and out at the back of his neck.
He lived about six hours, and when the sheriff asked whether he was Railroad Bill, he replied, "I may be, and I may not."
In his pockets were circulars announcing the reward for the outlaw, along with six dollars and a ticket to Pensacola, Florida.
Marshal Hardy took the body by train to Montgomery, where it arrived on the night of August 16 and a crowd pushed up to the depot to see the coffin opened.
Billie West, a Mr. Rowle and other railroad men who knew Railroad Bill "promptly agreed" that the body, "a large yellow negro" much lighter in complexion than the outlaw, was not his.
Other Louisville and Nashville employes were "in doubt," since his height, color, size and a scar under the left eye matched, and the body was decomposing.
A few days later E. Culpepper, a Black man of Chipley, wrote to Mrs. William Thomas of Mobile that the dead man was her husband and had said so on his deathbed.
Culpepper's letter said that "the colored people here" wanted to know whether there had been any crime against him.

Mrs. Thomas said her husband, a vessel loader, had lost his job in late July, when a disorderly-conduct warrant was issued against him, and had gone to Georgia to find work; she said he did not know Railroad Bill.
Reports from Mobile said no crime was charged against him there.
No report of an inquest, or of any charge against Garner, appears in the coverage.
The story reached white readers as news of an outlaw's possible end, under headlines such as "Is Railroad Bill Defunct?" in the Savannah Morning News.
That paper called Garner "a young sheriff's officer," called the dead man "the darkey," and gave only the shooters' account.
The Birmingham Age-Herald framed the Montgomery viewing as a spectacle, "What the Crowd Went to the Depot to See," and reported that the identification failed.
Three days later the Age-Herald printed the widow's account under the heading "The Identity of That Negro," giving her description of him as a "hard working, well behaved" man.
A Sumter, South Carolina, digest on August 21 and a syndicated item in Arkansas and Mississippi papers on August 23 and 24 still called him the probable outlaw.
No coverage of the killing was found in the Black press.

The Savannah dispatch and the Sumter digest named the shooter as Willis Garner of the sheriff's posse; the Age-Herald described an unnamed deputy constable and a young companion; the syndicated item spoke of "the four-cornered fight."
The Sumter digest dated the killing to Wednesday, while both Montgomery dispatches placed it on Thursday, August 15.

Accounts of his identity ran from Railroad Bill to "Thomas, the man who killed the Florida sheriff" to the Mobile laborer Thomas; the Montgomery viewing and the Culpepper letter were the most direct evidence.

accounts.label: Montgomery dispatch (Savannah Morning News)
accounts.gist: Willis Garner of the sheriff's posse found the man in a deserted house; the man shot Garner first and Garner, after falling, shot him through the chest; railroad employes were in doubt about the identity.

accounts.label: Montgomery special (Birmingham Age-Herald)
accounts.gist: A deputy constable and a young man went to an abandoned hut and called on the man to surrender; he shot the young man, who rose and killed him with a Winchester; railroad men who knew Railroad Bill said the body was not his.

accounts.label: Culpepper letter and the widow's account
accounts.gist: A Chipley man wrote that the dying man confessed to being the husband of Mrs. William Thomas of Mobile; she said he had gone to Georgia to hunt work and did not know Railroad Bill.

accounts.label: Syndicated item
accounts.gist: Marshal Hardy carried the body to Montgomery after Willis Garner killed the man 'in the four-cornered fight'; he was believed to be Railroad Bill.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headlined 'Is Railroad Bill Defunct?' and presented the shooters' version as fact, calling the dead man 'the darkey' and Garner 'a young sheriff's officer.'

The Birmingham Age-Herald framed the depot viewing as a spectacle ('Is What the Crowd Went to the Depot to See') and reported the identification failed; three days later it printed the widow's claim that he was a hard-working man with no crime charged.
A news-digest paragraph and a syndicated item, 'Thought to Be "Railroad Bill,"' still presented the dead man as probably the outlaw after the Montgomery identification had failed.
